question: What is the difference between a sightseeing cruise and a hop-on hop-off cruise?
answer: A sightseeing cruise is a single round-trip from your departure pier (usually Westminster or Tower) back to the same pier, with live commentary throughout. A hop-on hop-off cruise uses the same boats but lets you get off at any pier along the route — Westminster, Waterloo, Bankside, Tower, or Greenwich — and reboard a later boat. If you only want the view and commentary, the sightseeing cruise is simpler and usually cheaper.

question: Why do I need to book my departure time in advance?
answer: The Thames sees millions of river cruise passengers a year, and popular departures — especially weekend afternoons and summer evenings — can sell out. During peak season (June–September), popular sailing times can sell out 2–3 days in advance. Booking online beforehand guarantees your spot on your preferred departure and avoids arriving at the pier to find it fully booked.

question: What are the cruise departure times and how often do boats run?
answer: Most operators run cruises year-round, every 20–40 minutes during daytime hours, typically from around 10:00am to 6:00pm in summer and a slightly reduced schedule in winter. Evening cruises generally depart between 7:00pm and 9:30pm. Always check your ticket confirmation for the exact departure time and pier.

question: Do Thames river cruises operate in the rain or in winter?
answer: Yes — most Thames cruise boats have a covered, heated lower deck as well as an open-air upper deck, so cruises run in light rain and throughout the winter months. Cruises are only cancelled in severe weather (high winds, storms) or exceptionally high river levels, in which case you'll be offered a full refund or a free rebooking.

question: What is the difference between a Westminster departure and a Tower departure?
answer:
Both are popular starting piers along the same river, but the views differ:
  • Westminster Pier: Right next to Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament — cruises heading downstream pass the London Eye, the Southbank, and Tower Bridge.
  • Tower Pier: Beside the Tower of London — cruises heading downstream continue toward Greenwich and Canary Wharf, or upstream back past Tower Bridge toward Westminster.
Many round-trip sightseeing cruises depart from Westminster since it covers the most famous landmarks in one loop.

question: How do I get to the departure piers?
answer: Westminster Pier is a 2-minute walk from Westminster Underground station (Circle, District, Jubilee lines). Tower Pier is a 5-minute walk from Tower Hill station (Circle, District lines) or Tower Gateway (DLR). Greenwich Pier sits right next to Cutty Sark DLR station. All three piers are well signposted from their nearest station.

question: How much do Thames river cruise tickets cost?
answer: A standard 1-hour sightseeing cruise starts around £15 per adult. Guided cruises with live commentary run around £25, evening cruises with live music around £35, and the afternoon tea cruise (which includes food) around £55. Booking online in advance also lets you lock in your preferred departure time and often comes with a small discount versus buying at the pier.

question: How much time should I plan for a Thames cruise?
answer: A standard sightseeing cruise takes about 1 hour round-trip. If you want to include a stop in Greenwich, budget 2–3 hours for the round trip plus time exploring the Cutty Sark and Royal Observatory. The full-day combo (cruise, Tower Bridge, and Greenwich) takes roughly 6–7 hours in total.

question: Are prams, wheelchairs, or large luggage allowed onboard?
answer: Most Thames cruise boats are wheelchair accessible with a ramp at the pier and step-free access to the main deck — it's worth confirming accessibility with your specific operator when booking. Prams and pushchairs are welcome. Large suitcases are generally discouraged due to limited storage space onboard; a day bag or small backpack is fine.
